title: Balushahi
description: Balushahi is a classic North Indian halwai-style mithai known for its crisp, flaky layers, rich ghee flavor, soft interior, and delicate sugar glaze. The authentic texture comes from a short, lightly mixed dough, slow frying at a controlled temperature, and coating in properly cooked one-string sugar syrup.

ingredients.title: For the Balushahi Dough
items: Cold or room-temperature water – approximately 150–175 ml, as required

ingredients.title: For Frying
items: Ghee – 50% combined with neutral cooking oil, or pure ghee for a premium halwai-style version

ingredients.title: For the Sugar Syrup
items: Lemon juice – ½ tsp (2–3 ml), used sparingly

instruction.title: Step 1 – Preparing the Dough
steps: Sift maida, baking powder, baking soda, and salt into a wide mixing bowl.
Add 125 g desi ghee and rub it thoroughly into the flour with your fingertips until the mixture resembles coarse, damp sand.
Check the moyan by squeezing a handful of the flour mixture; it should hold its shape when compressed.
Mix the yogurt with approximately 150 ml water and gradually add it to the flour.
Bring the mixture together into a very soft, slightly rough dough. Do not knead or develop the gluten.
Add a little more water only if necessary. The dough should remain soft and loose rather than smooth and elastic.
Cover and rest the dough for 20–30 minutes.

instruction.title: Step 2 – Shaping the Balushahi
steps: After resting, gently bring the dough together once or twice without kneading.
Divide the dough into approximately 35–40 g portions for uniform pieces.
Gently roll each portion into a ball without applying excessive pressure.
Flatten each ball slightly with the palm of your hand.
Press the center with your thumb to create a shallow depression. Do not make a complete hole through the dough.
Keep the shaped Balushahi covered while preparing the frying fat.

instruction.title: Step 3 – Slow Frying
steps: Heat the ghee or ghee-oil mixture to approximately 140–150°C. The fat should be warm rather than very hot.
Carefully place the Balushahi into the frying fat without overcrowding the kadai.
Allow the pieces to cook slowly; they will initially sink and gradually rise as they fry.
Maintain a low, steady temperature and gently move the pieces occasionally for even cooking.
Fry for approximately 12–18 minutes, depending on size, until deeply golden, crisp, and evenly cooked.
Avoid high-temperature frying, as it can brown the exterior too quickly while leaving the center undercooked.
Remove the Balushahi and allow excess fat to drain.

instruction.title: Step 4 – Preparing the Sugar Syrup
steps: Combine 500 g sugar and 200–225 ml water in a heavy-bottomed pan.
Heat gently until the sugar dissolves completely, then bring the syrup to a steady boil.
Add ½ tsp lemon juice once the syrup has begun boiling. Use lemon juice sparingly so the syrup can still develop the characteristic Balushahi sugar coating.
Cook until one-string consistency (ek taar) is reached, approximately 105–110°C.
Test by taking a small amount of syrup between your thumb and index finger after cooling it enough to handle safely; it should form one continuous thin thread.
Add lightly crushed cardamom and optional rose water, then remove from the heat.

instruction.title: Step 5 – Sugar Coating
steps: Allow the fried Balushahi to cool and drain for several minutes before coating.
Keep the prepared syrup warm but not boiling, approximately 50–60°C.
Place the Balushahi into the warm syrup and gently turn each piece to coat it evenly.
Allow the pieces to remain in the syrup for approximately 3–5 minutes rather than soaking them for a prolonged period.
Remove and arrange the Balushahi on a clean tray without stacking.
Allow the sugar coating to cool and crystallize naturally on the surface.
For a thicker halwai-style coating, apply a second light coating after the first layer has begun to set.

instruction.title: Step 6 – Finishing
steps: Garnish lightly with finely sliced pistachios or almonds while the glaze is still slightly tacky.
Optional: finish with a few strands of saffron for a premium presentation.
Allow the Balushahi to rest until the sugar coating is completely set.
Serve at room temperature.

servingSuggestions.title: Serving Suggestions
items: Serve at room temperature as a traditional Indian mithai.
Pair with masala chai, cardamom tea, or unsweetened Indian tea.
For festive presentation, arrange in individual paper cups or on a mithai platter.
Balushahi is best enjoyed after the sugar coating has fully set and the exterior has become crisp.

chefTips: Do not knead the dough. Overworking develops gluten and produces a hard, bready Balushahi instead of a flaky halwai-style texture.
The correct moyan is essential. The flour and ghee mixture should hold together when squeezed before adding the liquid.
Keep the dough soft and slightly rough; a smooth, elastic dough indicates excessive mixing.
Fry slowly at approximately 140–150°C. Low-temperature frying cooks the center while developing the characteristic flaky exterior.
Do not overcrowd the kadai, as this lowers the frying temperature and can make the Balushahi greasy.
Use bone-dry, properly measured ingredients and consistent 35–40 g portions for uniform commercial batches.
For the sugar syrup, use only a small amount of lemon juice. Excess acid can make the coating sticky and interfere with the desired crystallization.
Cook the syrup to one-string consistency. Thin syrup produces a wet glaze, while excessively thick syrup creates an overly heavy sugar shell.
Keep the syrup warm rather than boiling when coating the fried Balushahi.
The finished Balushahi should have a crisp, flaky outer shell, irregular layers inside, a tender center, and a delicate sugar coating.
For a premium halwai version, use desi ghee for both the dough and frying, or a controlled ghee-oil blend for a more economical commercial batch.
